title: Overview of the TAC 2008 Update Summarization Task
research_question: How effectively can automatic systems produce concise summaries containing new information from a later document set when the reader is assumed to know an earlier set, and how well do automatic summary metrics reflect human judgments of that capability?
methodology: TAC 2008 defined 48 topics from the AQUAINT-2 English newswire collection; for each topic, 20 chronologically ordered documents were divided into an initial set of 10 and a later set of 10. Systems produced a 100-word initial summary and a 100-word update summary intended to avoid information already available from the earlier documents. All 71 submitted runs were scored with ROUGE and Basic Elements metrics, while 57 runs received manual evaluation for readability, overall responsiveness, and Pyramid content coverage; ANOVA, multiple-comparison tests, and correlation analyses were used to compare systems, humans, summary types, and metrics.

key_findings.finding: Human summaries were significantly better than automatic summaries on manual measures of readability, Pyramid content coverage, and overall responsiveness.
Human summarizers performed similarly on initial and update summaries, whereas automatic systems had greater difficulty selecting responsive content for the later update summaries.

The Pyramid evaluation explicitly rewarded coverage of weighted information units while giving no extra credit for repeating the same Summary Content Unit, thereby operationalizing both content completeness and non-redundancy.

ROUGE-2, ROUGE-SU4, and BE-HM correlated highly with manual evaluation for automatic summaries, and differences among their Pearson or Spearman correlations were not statistically significant at the 95 percent level.

Automatic overlap metrics failed to reproduce some important distinctions visible to manual evaluation, including the clear human-versus-system gap, and BE-HM failed to detect the aggregate degradation from initial to update summaries.

limitations: Only 57 of 71 submitted runs received the full manual evaluation.
Each topic's summaries were evaluated by a single assessor, who was also one of the human summarizers and usually the topic developer.
There were only eight human peers compared with many more automatic peers, making some human-side correlation estimates sparse.
The benchmark is restricted to English newswire, two fixed temporal batches, and 100-word summaries.
The two-cycle setup does not represent indefinitely evolving streams, superseded facts, or long-running work-item state.
ROUGE and Basic Elements depend heavily on lexical or structural overlap and can penalize valid paraphrases.
The task models a generic reader rather than adaptive user-specific priorities or personalized reminder value.
raw_claims: Each topic contained two chronological sets of ten newswire documents.
The second 100-word summary was supposed to communicate information that was new relative to the first document set.
Forty-eight evaluation topics were constructed by eight NIST assessors.
Seventy-one submitted runs received automatic ROUGE and Basic Elements scores.
Fifty-seven submitted runs received manual readability, content, and responsiveness evaluation.
Pyramid content units were weighted by how many reference summaries expressed the same information.
Repeated expression of the same Pyramid content unit did not earn additional credit.
Human summaries clearly outperformed automatic summaries on the manual quality measures.
Automatic systems performed worse on update summaries than on initial summaries, while the same degradation was not observed for human summaries.
ROUGE and Basic Elements correlations alone did not capture all of the discriminative behavior of human evaluation.
